title: CV-QKD with noisy coherent states and realistic displacement receivers
authors: L. F. Melo, J. J. Lacerda, John A. Mora Rodríguez, Alexandre B. Tacla
abstract: Near-optimal binary coherent state discrimination can be achieved by performing a displacement operation followed by photon detection. This displacement serves as a control parameter that can be tuned to optimize a chosen figure of merit, which makes such receivers attractive beyond state discrimination. Here, we turn this discrimination strategy into a complete continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) protocol based on a binary alphabet of noisy coherent states (displaced thermal states) and displacement receivers. We develop a strategy for estimating the channel parameters with the same displacement receiver, since standard quadrature-based methods do not apply. While a key map can be obtained with on/off detection, we demonstrate that reliable parameter estimation requires photon-number-resolving detection with sufficient resolution. Finite detector resolution underestimates the observed noise and constitutes a potential security loophole, which we quantify and show to be mitigable with modest resolution. We analyze the protocol's security against entangling-cloner collective attacks in the asymptotic regime, for both direct and reverse reconciliation, and show that it can generate secret keys even under noisy state preparation and imperfect detection. Interestingly, we find that the displacement that minimizes the discrimination error probability also performs well for key generation, thus providing a useful and analytically tractable tuning strategy for the CV-QKD receiver. We evaluate the protocol's performance over a range of transmittances and noise parameters, showing that the displacement receiver can outperform conventional homodyne detection in experimentally relevant regimes. Together, our results point to displacement receivers as a promising alternative for CV-QKD implementations.
summary: This work proposes a CV-QKD protocol using noisy coherent states and a displacement receiver, demonstrating its potential to outperform standard homodyne detection. The authors provide a full security analysis against collective attacks and derive a method to estimate channel parameters using realistic photon-number-resolving detection. This establishes the displacement receiver as a promising, robust alternative for quantum key distribution implementations.
main_problem: The paper develops and analyzes a Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution (CV-QKD) protocol utilizing a binary alphabet of noisy coherent states and displacement receivers.
main_result: The displacement receiver can outperform conventional homodyne detection in experimentally relevant regimes, and the protocol remains secure even with noisy state preparation and imperfect detection.
method: The security analysis is performed using the Devetak-Winter formula against entangling-cloner attacks, while parameter estimation is achieved by analyzing ratios of conditional probabilities derived from PNR measurements.
model_or_system: The system models quantum communication over a thermal-loss channel, using noisy coherent states (displaced thermal states) as the encoding basis and a displacement receiver for measurement.
key_observables: Secret key rate, discrimination error probability, channel transmittance ($\sqrt{\eta}$), and mutual information $I(A; B)$.
important_parameters: Transmissivity ($\eta$), noise parameters ($ ar{n}_A,  ar{n}_E$), detector efficiency ($\gamma$), and displacement parameter ($ eta$).
main_assumptions: The security analysis assumes a Gaussian channel model for Eve's information and that Alice's devices are trusted; reliable parameter estimation requires Photon-Number-Resolving (PNR) detection.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the prepare and measure scheme under an entangling-cloner collective attack, and Table I provides reference values for Eve's thermal mode mean photon number.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical model and the advantage of the displacement receiver for state discrimination. It then details the security analysis using the Devetak-Winter formula for key rate calculation. Finally, it develops methods for parameter estimation, deriving $\sqrt{\eta}$ by analyzing ratios of conditional probabilities from PNR measurements.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, experimentally relevant alternative to standard homodyne detection for CV-QKD, offering a tunable receiver strategy that improves performance in realistic noisy environments.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Prepare and measure scheme of the protocol under entangling-cloner collective attack. Alice prepares mode A and sends it through the quantum channel. Eve couples Al- ice’s mode to mode E1 of a two-mode squeezed vacuum state (TMSVS) on a beam-splitter with transmissivity η ∈[0, 1], which corresponds to the channel transmissivity. Eve keeps modes E′ 1 and E2 in a quantum memory for future measure- ments. The output mode B is sent to Bob, who performs a displacement operation followed by on/off detection.

FIG. 2. Secret key rate in reverse reconciliation at 50 km as a function of the quantum channel noise for displacement receivers with ideal detectors, assuming that Alice prepares states with ¯nA = 0.05 and the optimal amplitude for each receiver. The shaded region highlights the difference between the secret key rates of receivers (ii) and (iii), which vanishes at the crossover point ¯nE ≈1.8 × 10−3.

FIG. 3. Secret key rate in reverse reconciliation at 50 km as a function of the displacement β for different levels of channel noise. The stars, triangles, and circles correspond to the opti- mization of β for receivers (i), (ii) and (iii), respectively. Here, we consider α = 0.5, ¯nA = 0.05 and the values of ¯nE corre- spond to excess noise ξ = 0, 1.8×10−3, 9.0×10−3, 1.8×10−2, from top to bottom. The optimal displacement of receiver (ii) (β(ii) opt ≈0.35) is about half that of receiver (iii) (β(iii) opt ≈0.71). The interval β ∈(β(ii) opt , β(iii) opt ] (shaded region) corresponds to displacement values that achieve close-to-optimal secret key rates.

FIG. 4. Displacements for receivers (i), (ii) and (iii) as func- tions of distance for ¯nA = 0.05 and ¯nE = 10−4. For each re- ceiver, and at each distance, we use the amplitude that gives maximal secret key rate in reverse reconciliation. Inset shows the relative difference between the secret key rates obtained with the strategies bounding the shaded region. See text for details.
